title: To share or not to share: an experimental study on telematics adoption in an insurance setting
authors_or_outlet: Tommaso De Portu, Giancarlo Giudici; Journal of Financial Services Marketing
finding: A randomized vignette experiment with 1,301 European policyholders found transparent information modestly raised stated intent to buy telematics policies, and discounts and services substantially offset the privacy cost. Abstract only; stated intentions, European sample, no broker data.
atlas_use: Limited context on consumer trade-offs, not evidence about US data sales. The sample is outside the atlas's US focus.

title: Bridging the Gap: A Longitudinal Analysis of Extended Identifiers in the Post-Cookie Era
authors_or_outlet: Smith, Grossman, Franaszek, Torres-Agüero, Sen, Borcea, Chen; arXiv preprint
companies: PubCID | ID5 | Criteo | The Trade Desk | Audigent | LiveIntent | Lotame | 33Across | Yahoo | Quantcast | Neustar | Flashtalking | LinkedIn | Intimate Merger | PubMatic | BidSwitch | OpenX | Rubicon
finding: Across 145 million header bidding requests to six SSPs from 616,539 sites over 41 months, extended identifiers reached 83.76% of studied sites by May 2025. Twelve of 18 providers create IDs persistent across visits, sites, devices and months, 16 transmit them on EU sites without consent, and only one consistently recognized a self-identified bot crawler.
atlas_use: Main measurement of post-cookie identifiers and identity vendor reach in the bidstream, with evidence on ID accuracy. Disclose that two authors are affiliated with ad-verification firms Adalytics and DeepSee.io. LiveRamp and UID2 do not appear in the text, so it should not be cited for RampID prevalence.
quote: 12 of the providers create persistent EIDs

title: Extract, Violate, and Scare: Data Mining Tools Take Over the Immigration Surveillance State
finding: Uses LexisNexis Risk Solutions and monitoring contractor BI Inc. as case studies of private firms helping ICE track non-citizens while avoiding legal limits and oversight. Reports signs of fear, distress and trauma in immigrant communities.
atlas_use: Recent scholarly framing of LexisNexis as an immigration surveillance supplier and of community-level harm. Read at abstract level.
quote: extractivist corporations of the digital age mine large amounts of data from non-citizens

title: FTC announces proposed $2.25M settlement with tenant screening company over alleged FCRA violations
finding: Law firm summary of a proposed $2.25 million FTC penalty in D.D.C., announced 2026-07-09. Alleged failures include duplicate criminal and eviction entries, incomplete source disclosure, unforwarded disputes, and misleading statements about dispute outcomes. The company neither admits nor denies, and the order needs court entry.
atlas_use: Most recent FTC tenant screening action. Prefer the FTC release as the citation: https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2026/07/rentgrow-pay-225-million-settle-ftc-allegations-company-violated-fair-credit-reporting-act-ftc-act. Court approval is still unconfirmed.
quote: permitting the same criminal conviction or eviction proceeding to appear as multiple separate entries

title: The Eviction Caste System
authors_or_outlet: Allison M. Freedman; Boston College Law Review 67(5)
finding: Law review article proposing an eviction caste framework, with a section arguing that tenant screening companies sell inaccurate and incomplete data that brands renters with a lasting 'Scarlet E'. Its notes cite secondary sources on CoreLogic's SafeRent Score and a TransUnion survey of landlords.
atlas_use: Secondary legal framing and a route to further case citations. Vendor names appear in footnotes, not as original findings about those vendors.

title: The legal tech giants powering ICE, part 1: how Thomson Reuters and LexisNexis helped support America's immigration surveillance machine
companies: Thomson Reuters | LexisNexis Risk Solutions | Appriss Insights
finding: Reports DHS's CLEAR access was renewed on a sole-source justification around March 2026, under a contract separate from the $22.8 million LEIDS-5 deal, per a post-publication correction. The $22.1 million LexisNexis contract is listed as completed with no confirmed successor. Thomson Reuters says CLEAR lacks citizenship and immigration status data.
atlas_use: Most current status of both contracts, with pointers to USAspending records. Verify values and end dates there. The article has several later edits, and renewal length is unconfirmed.
quote: Thomson Reuters’ $22.8 million ICE contract is set to expire on May 31, 2026

title: MASSIVE WIN FOR PLAINTIFFS: Federal Court Keeps Wiretap and FCRA Claims Alive in Allstate/Arity Software Development Kit Tracking Class Action—Right on the Heels of the Texas AG Lawsuit
authors_or_outlet: Tori Guidry, Troutman Amin LLP, in National Law Review (republished from CIPAWorld)
finding: Summarizes the March 3, 2026 N.D. Ill. pleading-stage ruling (No. 25 CV 407): wiretap, FCRA claims against Arity, pen register and some privacy and consumer claims survive, while computer hacking, New York SHIELD Act and Pennsylvania privacy claims fall. Nothing has been finally decided on the merits. The author's tone favors plaintiffs, so the opinion itself should be pulled.
atlas_use: Status marker for private litigation over SDK-collected driving data, and a lead to the opinion at 2026 WL 594708.
quote: creates massive legal exposure under the FCRA and wiretap statutes

title: Connecticut Fair Housing Center v. CoreLogic Rental Property Solutions, LLC, Nos. 23-1118(L), 23-1166(XAP)
authors_or_outlet: US Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
finding: Private litigation, not agency enforcement. The panel held the fair housing group lacked standing and that the Fair Housing Act does not categorically exclude types of actors, but CoreLogic did not cause the housing denial here, so no prima facie disparate-impact case. It reversed FCRA liability because the certificate provided was facially invalid, so the documentation rules could not be shown to have blocked file access.
atlas_use: Important counterweight: limits screener disparate-impact liability, and should be cited alongside the harm evidence. Holdings were checked against the opinion's syllabus and targeted passages, not every page.
quote: CoreLogic did not cause the denial of housing in this case

title: Devilish devs spawn 287 Chrome extensions to flog your browser history to data brokers
companies: Similarweb | Big Star Labs | Semrush | Alibaba Group | ByteDance
finding: Reports a pseudonymous researcher's test harness that matched outbound requests to synthetic browsing and flagged 287 extensions with about 37.4 million installs leaking visited URLs to more than 30 recipients. For about 20 million installs the collector was unknown. Similarweb did not respond; its policy discloses collection and says some data may be personal and sensitive.
atlas_use: Most recent evidence on clickstream supply. It is one researcher's unreviewed report as covered by press, and the underlying report was not read, so verify it before stating counts as fact.
quote: you should assume you are the product

title: Class action claims Checkr misreported criminal records in background checks (Davis v. Checkr Inc., No. 0:26-cv-60088)
finding: Reports a proposed nationwide FCRA class action in S.D. Fla. alleging Checkr attached other people's criminal records to consumer reports and lacked reasonable accuracy procedures. These are unproven allegations in a complaint.
atlas_use: Marks Checkr as having pending accuracy litigation, worded as allegation only. Verify on the docket.

title: FTC Finalizes Order Settling Allegations that GM and OnStar Collected and Sold Geolocation Data Without Consumers' Informed Consent
finding: The final order bars GM for five years from giving geolocation and driver behavior data to consumer reporting agencies. Over its 20-year life it requires affirmative express consent with limited exceptions, a way to request a copy or deletion of data, and an opt-out from collection. Where the vehicle technology allows, consumers must also be able to disable precise geolocation collection.
atlas_use: Anchor enforcement record for connected-car data, and a source for the rights drivers now hold against GM.
quote: GM's egregious betrayal of consumers' trust

title: Justice Department Requires RealPage to End the Sharing of Competitively Sensitive Information and Alignment of Pricing Among Competitors
authors_or_outlet: US Department of Justice, Antitrust Division
finding: The proposed settlement bars RealPage from using rivals' nonpublic data in live rent-setting, limits model training to nonpublic data at least 12 months old, and ends market surveys collecting sensitive data. It was filed in M.D.N.C. and was subject to court approval.
atlas_use: Shows landlord data pooling as a data flow and a remedy. This is antitrust rather than FCRA, so frame it that way. Confirm final entry on the docket.
quote: Competing companies must make independent pricing decisions

title: Exceptions in the Algorithmic Age: Evidence from the Case of Tenant Screening
authors_or_outlet: Barbara Kiviat, Sara Sternberg Greene, Hesu Yoon; American Journal of Sociology 131(4)
finding: Interviews with landlords, property managers and screening executives show gatekeepers deciding which records to overlook, and that algorithmic screening requires exceptions to be codified in advance. Applicants whose circumstances are culturally salient and institutionally legible are the ones who benefit.
atlas_use: Qualitative evidence on how screening rules decide who gets leniency. Read from the abstract only; the page itself was not opened.

title: Dun & Bradstreet Faces $5.7 Million Penalty for Failing to Honor FTC Order
finding: Reports that D&B agreed to pay $5.7 million, about $3.7 million in refunds and over $2 million in civil penalties, over alleged violations of the 2022 order. The alleged breaches involved renewal price disclosure, claims that paid products raise credit scores, and missing call recordings.
atlas_use: Shows repeat conduct after the 2022 order. Secondary source, and the allegations concern sales practices rather than data accuracy; replace with the FTC release when it is located.
quote: Our signed orders are not suggestions.

title: 'Cookie-less' identification for/against privacy?
authors_or_outlet: Sivan-Sevilla, Parham, McGuigan; Internet Policy Review 14(3)
finding: Sorts first-party identification into Universal IDs, Onboarding IDs and Walled Garden IDs and tests each against five cookie-era privacy concerns. It concludes that UID2 and RampID keep cross-site tracking in some form, lengthen tracking through persistence, and offer doubtful opt-out and transparency.
atlas_use: Ready-made taxonomy for an identity-graph category in the atlas, with a sourced critique of both UID2 and RampID architectures.
quote: first-party identification actually intensifies important aspects of online surveillance

title: The ICE–Lexis nexus: An argument against use of commercial databases in immigration enforcement
authors_or_outlet: Jessica P. Needle, Alan Rubel; Big Data & Society
finding: Philosophical argument, built around the Castellanos v. LexisNexis complaint, that US government use of Accurint is morally objectionable and that its use for noncriminal immigration enforcement is unjustifiable. It gives an argument and allegations, not new measurement.
atlas_use: Citation for the ethics of LexisNexis-ICE use and a pointer to the Castellanos litigation and the Accurint product. Read the full text before relying on details.

title: Taxpayer Identity Verification: IRS Should Strengthen Oversight of Its Identity-Proofing Program (GAO-25-107273)
finding: GAO finds ID.me is the IRS's only provider at the second identity assurance level, with over 150 million application accesses from 2021 through 2024. The IRS could not show measurable goals or documented routine performance reviews, and had not logged ID.me's AI use in its inventory.
atlas_use: Strongest independent evidence on ID.me's government role and on oversight gaps. The page shows three recommendations open and one implemented. Re-check at each monthly refresh.
quote: IRS relies on one vendor, ID.me, to prove taxpayers' identities

title: LexisNexis C.L.U.E. & Telematics OnDemand
finding: The CFPB lists LexisNexis C.L.U.E. as holding up to seven years of auto claims and seven years of home and personal property claims, and Telematics OnDemand as holding driving behavior data for auto pricing. It sets out a free report every 12 months, freezes on request and FCRA disputes. The date is the page's last-updated date.
atlas_use: Concrete consumer route for LexisNexis insurance files: how to get a report, freeze it and dispute errors.
quote: Fact-check your specialty insurance report when applying for insurance.

title: Citing 'Sufficiently Pleaded' Allegations, Judge Won't Toss Online Consent Dispute
finding: Reports that a federal judge in Washington state denied ZoomInfo's motions to dismiss and to strike class allegations in a suit alleging it uses names without consent to advertise its database. This is a pleading-stage ruling only.
atlas_use: Shows a consent dispute was live in 2025. Only the lead paragraph is visible, and the plaintiff name LaRock is inferred from an attachment title, so check the docket for names and later status.
quote: her name is used by ZoomInfo to do more than merely describe

title: Are more lead gen providers disappearing from LinkedIn?
finding: Reports Apollo.io and Seamless.AI company pages vanished from LinkedIn around March 6, 2025, and notes their Chrome extensions pull profile data. Apollo's CEO called it a brand page restriction with no service impact; the article has no statement from LinkedIn. A LinkedIn post it cites claimed four firms were removed for scraping.
atlas_use: Evidence that browser extensions are a B2B collection route. Do not state that LinkedIn banned them for scraping: LinkedIn gave no reason in this article, and a later return of Apollo's page was not verified.
quote: does not disrupt Apollo's services or impact our core platform functionality

title: The Primary Care Medical Record Industry in Canada and Its Data Collection and Commercialization Practices
authors_or_outlet: Spithoff, Vesely, McPhail, Rowe, Mogic, Grundy; JAMA Network Open
finding: Using 19 interviews and 22 public documents, the study describes two broker models: de-identifying clinic records to sell analytics, and owning clinics and using sponsored algorithms to flag patients who may qualify for a sponsor's drug. Pharmaceutical companies were the main clients. The studied brokers appear unnamed in this account, while IQVIA is named as background.
atlas_use: Rare empirical study of how the health data broker business works and a useful business-model taxonomy. Canadian scope, so use as comparison rather than US evidence.
quote: Patients are notably absent from decision-making

title: Coalition letter supporting the Homebuyers Privacy Protection Act (S. 1467, H.R. 2808)
authors_or_outlet: Housing and financial services coalition, hosted by Consumer Federation of America
finding: Explains that a lender's mortgage credit inquiry alerts the credit reporting agency, which sells that signal onward as a trigger lead without the consumer's knowledge or approval. Signatories mix consumer groups with banking, mortgage and real estate trade groups, so it is not purely independent.
atlas_use: Closest source on home-buying data resale. No credit bureau is named. Whether and when the bill became law needs a primary check; the letter predates enactment.
quote: sold to data brokers (including other lenders)

title: Lawsuit Alleges GM Illegally Sold Arkansans' Driving Data to Insurance Companies
finding: Describes the Arkansas Attorney General complaint's account of the pipeline: a 2015 GM agreement to sell to Verisk, a Verisk telematics exchange, and driving scores insurers could look up for current or prospective policyholders. All of this is as alleged in the complaint.
atlas_use: Explains the mechanism linking automaker to broker score to insurer, and fills in the broker name the AG release omits.
quote: Verisk established a telematics data exchange to house the driver data received from GM

title: Attorney General Griffin Sues General Motors and OnStar for Deceiving Arkansans and Unlawfully Selling Data
finding: State suit under the Deceptive Trade Practices Act, plus unjust enrichment, alleges driving data was sold to unnamed third parties who passed it to insurers, who then denied coverage or raised rates. These are allegations, and the release names no broker. Later status was not found.
atlas_use: State-level enforcement entry beside the FTC order, which shows a separate liability track.
quote: We will hold GM accountable for deceiving Arkansans

title: Brooks et al. v. Thomson Reuters (case page, $27.5 million settlement over CLEAR)
finding: Private class action under California's Unfair Competition Law and privacy law, alleging CLEAR collected and sold Californians' data without knowledge or consent. The class was certified and a $27.5 million settlement with injunctive relief won final approval in February 2025.
atlas_use: Enforcement-style entry for CLEAR, but it is private litigation, not agency action, and the source is plaintiffs' counsel. Pull the final approval order from the docket for the injunctive terms, which this page omits.
quote: cradle-to-grave dossiers on each person

title: Allstate accused of quietly paying app makers for driver data
companies: Arity | Allstate | Life360 | GasBuddy | Fuel Rewards | Routely | Toyota | Lexus | Mazda | Chrysler | Dodge | Fiat | Jeep | Maserati | Ram
finding: Report on the Texas complaint: an Arity SDK in apps collected location, sensor and trip data, which was allegedly combined with licensed personal data and used to justify rate rises, denials or dropped coverage. Automaker purchases are also alleged. Allstate's spokesperson says Arity helps with accurate pricing after consent.
atlas_use: Named apps and manufacturers for mapping phone-based driving data flows into Arity. All are allegations. It adds names to the Record article already in the sources.

title: A large-scale study of performance and equity of commercial remote identity verification technologies across demographics
authors_or_outlet: Fatima, Schuckers, Cruz-Ortiz, Hou, Purnapatra, Andrews, Neupane, Marshall, Schuckers; IEEE IJCB 2024
finding: Tests five commercial remote ID checks on 3,991 subjects. Two were equitable across all demographics. One had higher false rejections for Black/African American participants and darker skin tones, and another performed inequitably in favor of the AAPI group.
atlas_use: Independent evidence that document-and-selfie checks can fail unevenly. The abstract does not name vendors, so it must not be attributed to Socure, Jumio or ID.me. Only the abstract and arXiv page were read, not the full paper.
quote: Two of the RIdV solutions were equitable across all demographics

title: Uncovering Digital Trace Data Biases: Tracking Undercoverage in Web Tracking Data
authors_or_outlet: Oriol J. Bosch, Patrick Sturgis, Jouni Kuha; Communication Methods and Measures
finding: Using panels in Spain, Portugal and Italy, the authors found that most participants in commercial web tracking panels had devices or browsers left untracked, and simulations show this can substantially bias estimates of online media exposure. Device use, more than personal traits, drove the gap.
atlas_use: Independent accuracy caveat for panel-based web data generally. It does not test Similarweb or Comscore and is not US data. Read through the OpenAlex abstract only.
quote: more than 70% of participants affected

title: Socure explains identity verification compliance to 2 state lawmakers
finding: Reports Socure's replies to lawmakers in New York and Virginia: it says it does not sell data or use it for marketing, is not a data broker under New York law, and complies with state privacy laws.
atlas_use: The company's position on whether it is a data broker, reported by trade press. Treat these as Socure's claims, not verified facts; useful for classifying Socure cautiously.
quote: We are only focused on verifying identity and rooting out fraud

title: Senators Expose Car Companies' Terrible Data Privacy Practices
finding: Readout of the Wyden-Markey letter: Honda was paid about 26 cents per car and Hyundai about 61 cents by Verisk, which resold the data to insurers. It says GM stopped sharing driving data after the New York Times investigation but kept sharing location data, with no opt-out short of disabling connectivity.
atlas_use: Readable, accessible source for the per-car figures while the letter itself could not be fetched. The location-data de-identification line is EFF's opinion and should be attributed.
quote: there is no way to de-identify location data

title: Programmatic Companies Wrestle With ID Bridging And What Counts As Fraud
finding: Explains ID bridging as a publisher or vendor recognising a visitor when the cookie field is empty, sometimes inserting an alternative ID. IAB Tech Lab's proposed OpenRTB fields would disclose who created, inserted and matched a bridged ID, without banning the practice.
atlas_use: Usable plain definition of ID bridging, a topic where no peer-reviewed measurement was found. It reflects industry voices, not independent testing.

title: Katz-Lacabe et al. v. Oracle America, Inc. settlement agreement
authors_or_outlet: N.D. Cal. No. 3:22-cv-04792-RS, copy hosted by ClassAction.org
finding: Oracle funds a $115 million non-reversionary settlement for US residents whose data was collected by Oracle Advertising or made available through ID Graph or Data Marketplace. It will certify that it will not capture user-generated referrer URL information or, except on its own sites, online form text, and will run an audit program on customer compliance. Oracle denies all allegations and admits no liability.
atlas_use: Documents the legal exposure of a major identity graph and its product names, along with concrete collection limits. This is private class-action litigation rather than regulator action.
quote: not capture (a) user-generated information within referrer URLs

title: Letter of concern to New York CIO on the state's use of Socure
authors_or_outlet: NY State Sen. Jeremy A. Cooney (copy hosted by StateScoop)
finding: A state senator asks whether New York tested Socure's fraud models for bias, confirmed its 95% fraud-prevention claim, and verified privacy compliance. Cites a Rep. Torres letter and a former customer's suit alleging 31% prevention. These are questions and allegations, not findings.
atlas_use: Best located non-vendor document on Socure, useful for showing what is unanswered. Do not present its description of Socure as a data broker as established, and pair it with Socure's reply.
quote: Has the state tested Socure's fraud prediction models for bias

title: Adalytics Claims Colossus SSP Is Misdeclaring IDs In Its Bid Requests
companies: Colossus SSP | Direct Digital Holdings | The Trade Desk | BidSwitch | Criteo
finding: Reports Adalytics' claim that most impressions bought through Colossus on The Trade Desk carried an ID that did not match the browser, while 15 other SSPs matched every time. Colossus and BidSwitch each deny responsibility.
atlas_use: Shows that bidstream identifiers can be wrong or misdeclared. The dispute is contested and unadjudicated, so it should be attributed carefully and not stated as fact.

title: Proposed FTC Order will Prohibit Telehealth Firm Cerebral from Using or Disclosing Sensitive Data for Advertising Purposes
finding: The FTC alleged Cerebral sent sensitive data on nearly 3.2 million consumers to third parties including LinkedIn, Snapchat and TikTok through tracking tools. The settlement included nearly $5.1 million in refunds tied to cancellation practices and a $10 million penalty suspended after a $2 million payment.
atlas_use: Adds scale and a remedy to the health enforcement timeline. Ad-tech flow, not broker sale.

title: Vancouver tech company ZoomInfo proposes settlement of up to $29 million in 'right to publicity' lawsuits
finding: Reports ZoomInfo told investors it proposed settling putative class actions over use of Illinois and California residents' names on public web pages, at an estimated $26 million to $29 million.
atlas_use: Scale of consent litigation exposure. Local news reporting of an investor disclosure; final approval was not verified and a settlement is not an admission.

title: Meta v. Bright Data Ruling Has Important Implications for Webscraping Activities by Investment Advisers (IM)
authors_or_outlet: Scott H. Moss, Boris Liberman, George Danenhauer, Michael J. Scales; Lowenstein Sandler client alert
finding: Summarizes the January 23, 2024 N.D. Cal. summary judgment for Bright Data: no evidence of logged-in scraping and unclear contract terms on logged-out scraping. It tells advisers that account-linked scraping turns on the specific terms, and to run diligence on scraped-data vendors.
atlas_use: Connects scraping law directly to the alternative data buyer side. Law-firm commentary; cite the order itself for the holding.

title: The problem with criminal records: Discrepancies between state reports and private-sector background checks
finding: Comparing official state reports with regulated and unregulated private background checks for 101 people, the authors found at least one false positive for 60 and 50 percent of participants respectively, and at least one false negative for 90 and 92 percent.
atlas_use: Best independent accuracy figure for the screening category. The sample is small and the abstract names no vendors, so it supports a category-level claim only.
quote: private-sector background checks are laden with false-positive and false-negative errors

title: Pervasive identity surveillance for marketing purposes: A technical report on personal data processing for LiveRamp's 'RampID' identity graph system
authors_or_outlet: Wolfie Christl and Alan Toner; Cracked Labs, commissioned by Open Rights Group
finding: Using public software documentation and promotional material, it describes how AbiliTec links names, addresses, emails and phones and how RampID ties device and cookie IDs to that record. It reports identity records on about 700 million people globally and a LiveRamp-stated 60 billion daily RampID transmissions in the bidstream. The authors caution that documentation may be incomplete and client implementation is largely unclear.
atlas_use: Best independent mechanical description of how an identity graph operates. Scale figures should be attributed to LiveRamp's claims. The focus is Europe, with complaints filed in the UK and France. Acxiom appears only as LiveRamp's former name.
quote: private population registers

title: FTC and CFPB Settlement to Require Trans Union to Pay $15 Million over Charges It Failed to Ensure Accuracy of Tenant Screening Reports
companies: TransUnion Rental Screening Solutions | Trans Union LLC
finding: The agencies alleged inaccurate eviction records: developments in one case shown as several evictions, dismissed cases shown as merely filed or as landlord judgments, sealed records included, and claimed sums labelled as judgment amounts. The settlement is $11 million in redress plus a $4 million penalty, with the complaint filed in D. Colo.
atlas_use: Primary enforcement source for tenant screening accuracy, with concrete failure modes for eviction data.
quote: Consumers struggling to find housing shouldn’t be shut out by tenant screening reports

title: Massive Study on Matching Households and Email Addresses Finds Range of Inaccuracies
authors_or_outlet: Truthset, via ADWEEK Wire (unedited partner content)
finding: Truthset says that across 3.9 billion hashed email records from 15 data companies, email-to-postal links were right 51% of the time on average, ranging from 32% to 69% by provider.
atlas_use: Quantified evidence on hashed-email link accuracy, usable only as a labelled self-report. Truthset sells validation services, so it cannot be applied to any named broker.
quote: accurate 51% of the time

title: Martinez v. ZoomInfo Technologies, Inc., No. 22-35305 (9th Cir. panel opinion, reported as vacated)
authors_or_outlet: US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit (opinion by Judge McKeown)
finding: A union official sued because ZoomInfo showed a redacted teaser profile beside subscription links without her permission or payment. The panel affirmed denial of the anti-SLAPP motion on a public-interest exemption ground without reaching the publicity claim's merits. As pleaded, a free tier required handing over the names and contact details of everyone the subscriber had emailed. Search results report the opinion was vacated on the January 18, 2024 en banc grant and the case then settled.
atlas_use: Use only as a description of pleaded facts about how B2B directories use profiles as advertising and the contributed-contacts route. Do not cite as precedent. Private litigation, not agency enforcement.
quote: ZoomInfo did not obtain her permission or compensate her

title: Report Details Severe Credit Score Penalties in Auto Insurance
finding: CFA's release says clean-record drivers paid on average $470 with excellent credit and $1,012 with poor credit for state-mandated cover. It attributes disproportionately higher premiums for lower-income drivers and people of color to credit-based pricing, with no figures for that in the release. An advocacy source; the full report and its method were not read.
atlas_use: Quantified harm estimate for insurance scoring, attributed to CFA as an advocate.
quote: Your auto insurance premium should be based on your driving record

title: FTC to Ban BetterHelp from Revealing Consumers' Data, Including Sensitive Mental Health Information, to Facebook and Others for Targeted Advertising
finding: The FTC alleged BetterHelp disclosed email addresses, IP addresses and health questionnaire answers to Facebook, Snapchat, Criteo and Pinterest for advertising after promising limited use. The proposed order required $7.8 million for partial refunds.
atlas_use: Enforcement evidence for mental health data leaving a consumer service. Ad-tech flow, not broker sale.

title: FTC Enforcement Action to Bar GoodRx from Sharing Consumers' Sensitive Health Info for Advertising
finding: In its first Health Breach Notification Rule case, the FTC alleged the prescription discount service shared users' health information with Facebook, Google, Criteo and others despite contrary promises. The proposed order set a $1.5 million penalty and a permanent ban on advertising disclosure, subject to court approval.
atlas_use: Primary enforcement source for prescription data outside HIPAA. GoodRx is a source of ad-tech data flows rather than a data broker and should be labelled so.

title: What Recent Rulings in 'hiQ v. LinkedIn' and Other Cases Say About the Legality of Data Scraping
authors_or_outlet: The Recorder, reprinted by Farella Braun + Martel
finding: Explains that the Ninth Circuit held the CFAA does not reach automatic collection of public web data, while contract and other claims remain. LinkedIn won summary judgment on contract and unfair competition claims over hiQ's use of contractors with fake accounts to collect logged-in data.
atlas_use: Plain-language scraping law background. That these disputes give the profiled people no remedy is the atlas's own inference, not a statement in the article. Law-firm commentary, not the opinions.
quote: free rein to decide, on any basis, who can collect and use

title: Private Passenger Auto Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning Survey Results (NAIC Staff Report)
authors_or_outlet: National Association of Insurance Commissioners, survey technical team
companies: Verisk | LexisNexis Risk Solutions | TransUnion | CCC Intelligent Solutions | Cambridge Mobile Telematics
finding: The survey of auto insurers listed 2,531 AI/ML models, 42% developed by third parties, and 104 distinct third-party data sources. Few companies said they tell consumers about data elements beyond what law requires: for rating 23 yes (three of them models not yet implemented), 49 no, 121 blank; for claims 0 yes, 140 no, 53 blank.
atlas_use: Best regulator evidence for how widely insurers buy outside data and how little they disclose. Note it covers AI/ML models only and has many blank answers.
quote: There are 104 unique third parties listed as data sources in the survey.

title: ID.me misled IRS on processing times for identity verification, congressional investigators found
finding: Reports House Oversight investigators found ID.me told the IRS waits were about two hours while average waits exceeded four hours for 14 of 21 state unemployment agencies. They could not substantiate the CEO's $400 billion fraud claim. ID.me called the criticism of its fraud assessment premature and said delays were temporary.
atlas_use: Evidence of access harms when verification is outsourced. Secondary coverage; link the committee's document directly if located.
quote: inaccurately overstated its capacity to conduct identity verification services

title: CFPB Reports Highlight Problems with Tenant Background Checks
finding: Announces a market report and a consumer snapshot drawing on more than 24,000 complaints and focus groups with 44 renters. More than 16,000 complaints concerned incorrect information, about 4,500 concerned trouble fixing errors, and rental payment history covers only an estimated 1.7 to 2.3 percent of renters.
atlas_use: Regulator-level harm evidence. This is the press release, so cite the underlying reports once they are opened. No screening companies are named.

title: Which Information Matters? Measuring Landlord Assessment of Tenant Screening Reports
finding: In a behavioral experiment using simulated reports, landlords applied blanket policies, conflated eviction filings with executed evictions, and tended to defer to the scores shown. The author argues this produces disproportionate exclusion of renters of color.
atlas_use: Explains how report design turns weak records into denials. Read from the abstract only.
quote: tendencies toward automation bias

title: Leaky Forms: A Study of Email and Password Exfiltration Before Form Submission
authors_or_outlet: Senol, Acar, Humbert, Zuiderveen Borgesius; USENIX Security 2022
finding: A crawl of the top 100,000 sites found email addresses sent to tracking, marketing and analytics domains before form submission and without consent on 2,950 sites from the US vantage point and 1,844 from the EU. Forty-one receiving tracker domains were on no popular blocklist checked.
atlas_use: Evidence of how email identifiers, the raw material of email-based identity graphs, reach third parties without user action. It offers a useful US versus EU comparison.

title: Top IQVIA lawyer declines to discuss Experian relationship, but pledges Americans' medical secrets are safe
finding: IQVIA has bought financial and demographic data on tens of millions of Americans from Experian and uses it among sources including hospital records to give drug and device makers marketing insights. STAT says internal documents show staff questioned the safeguards on data covering more than 120 million people. Only the unpaywalled opening was read.
atlas_use: Strongest independent evidence of a credit bureau to health data broker link; supports a data-flow edge from Experian to IQVIA, attributed to STAT.

title: How a complex web of businesses turned private health records from GE into a lucrative portrait of patients
companies: Quintiles (now IQVIA) | GE Healthcare | Truven Health Analytics
finding: Quintiles took millions of de-identified GE Healthcare patient records and linked them to insurance claims. A confidential GE memo raised privacy concerns and said patients could be flagged in another dataset with near perfect accuracy. Paywalled; only the opening was read.
atlas_use: Documented case of commercial linkage of de-identified records. The conclusions about HIPAA should wait for the full article.
quote: at risk of privacy violations

title: Privacy as the Price of Drug Access
authors_or_outlet: Laura Karas, Science and Technology Law Review 23(1)
finding: Drug company patient support programs obtain linked patient and prescriber data through HIPAA authorizations, after which few limits apply to downstream use. The article argues this data can support kickback schemes and product hopping. Abstract read through OpenAlex.
atlas_use: Documents a pharmacy-adjacent collection channel that uses patient authorization rather than de-identification. Drug makers are not brokers, so this is context for health data flows.
quote: compel patients to trade protected health information for drug access

title: Letter from consumer and immigrant rights groups to CFPB urging FCRA coverage of credit header data
authors_or_outlet: National Consumer Law Center, Consumer Action, Consumer Federation of America, Consumer Reports, National Immigration Law Center, U.S. PIRG
companies: Equifax | Experian | TransUnion | National Consumer Telecom & Utilities Exchange (NCTUE)
finding: Traces the header exclusion to an FTC staff summary of the FCRA and argues CFPB can close it through guidance. Argues that a header list can itself reveal sensitive facts; a missing SSN or use of an ITIN, for example, can hint at immigration status.
atlas_use: Clear definition of credit header fields and of the legal theory for closing the gap. Date caveat: the letter is printed January 20, 2021, but it cites a December 2021 letter and PDF metadata shows January 2022, so 2022 is inferred.
quote: the very keys for identity theft

title: In Response to FTC Charges, Dun & Bradstreet to Clean Up Small Business Credit Reporting Process and Refund Customers
finding: The FTC alleged D&B gave businesses no clear, reliable way to fix errors in credit reports and sold CreditBuilder products with misleading claims and undisclosed auto-renewals. The proposed order required deletion or reinvestigation of disputed items, correction deadlines and refunds.
atlas_use: Best independent accuracy and correction evidence for D&B. Mark it as business credit files, not consumer data, so it is not read as a personal privacy finding.
quote: A faulty D&B credit report can be a huge burden on a small business

title: Unfair Collection: Reclaiming Control of Publicly Available Personal Information from Data Scrapers
authors_or_outlet: Andrew M. Parks, Michigan Law Review 120(5)
finding: A student Note arguing that California's CPRA lets scrapers collect, share and profit from public personal information outside regulation, and proposing GDPR-style notice requirements for scrapers.
atlas_use: Legal framing for why opt-out rights are weak for scraped profiles. It is an argument, read at abstract level only.
quote: leaves a wide-open gap for internet data scrapers

title: Letter from Sen. Ron Wyden to CFPB Director Chopra on credit-header data
authors_or_outlet: Office of Sen. Ron Wyden (copy hosted by CDIA)
companies: Equifax | Experian | TransUnion | National Consumer Telecom & Utilities Exchange (NCTUE) | Thomson Reuters
finding: Says bureaus sell names, addresses, birth dates and SSNs in bulk to brokers who resell to investigators and government. Reports that NCTUE let Equifax resell header data on 171 million people and keep the revenue, while utilities on NCTUE's board were unaware. NCTUE told Equifax to stop in October 2021, but brokers keep selling data already bought.
atlas_use: Primary source for the header-data flow from utilities to NCTUE, Equifax and a Thomson Reuters service used by ICE, including the 171 million figure. This is a senator's account from his own inquiry, so attribute it to him.
quote: these data brokers are serving as shady middlemen

title: Utility giants agree to no longer share sensitive records ICE used to track the public
authors_or_outlet: Drew Harwell, The Washington Post (repost by NNIRR)
companies: National Consumer Telecom & Utilities Exchange (NCTUE) | Equifax | Thomson Reuters
finding: Reports NCTUE agreed to stop licensing members' header data after Wyden's pressure, while earlier data stayed available. Equifax had licensed the data onward, and CLEAR bundled it for police, law firms and agencies including ICE.
atlas_use: Independent news corroboration of the Wyden letter and the point that past sales were not recalled. Read via a nonprofit's repost; link the original Post article if possible.
quote: The data never should have been used in this way.

title: SEC Charges App Annie and its Founder with Securities Fraud
finding: The SEC charged App Annie over conduct from late 2014 to mid-2018. The company agreed to a $10 million penalty and its co-founder to $300,000 and a three-year officer and director bar. The SEC called it its first case charging an alternative data provider with securities fraud.
atlas_use: Anchor enforcement item for the investor-data category; the harm is deceived data suppliers and investors, not consumers directly, and the case concerns company data. The order itself was not read.
quote: The federal securities laws prohibit deceptive conduct and material misrepresentations

title: Similarweb's controversial route to Wall Street
finding: Reports that until 2017 Similarweb gathered browsing data through software distributed in breach of Google and Mozilla terms, and that it bought the Stylish extension, removed from the stores after a researcher's 2018 findings. It then shifted toward paid data from partners such as telecoms and cybersecurity firms. Similarweb calls the allegations groundless and long refuted. Globes says current apps require specific user approval.
atlas_use: Sourcing history and ownership link for the Similarweb entry, including the company's rebuttal so the claim is presented as contested.

title: LexisNexis to Provide Giant Database of Personal Information to ICE
finding: Reports a $16.8 million ICE contract shared by Mijente, covering records including credit history, bankruptcies, license plate images and cell subscriber data. LexisNexis said the tool contains mainly public government records and that non-public data use is authorized by federal law.
atlas_use: Evidence of data types sold to government. The $16.8 million differs from the $22.1 million reported later by LawSites; show both with dates.
quote: exceedingly difficult to participate in modern society without generating computerized records

title: United States v. Epsilon Data Management, LLC (case page; DOJ release: Marketing Company Agrees to Pay $150 Million for Facilitating Elder Fraud Schemes)
authors_or_outlet: US Department of Justice, Civil Division
finding: Epsilon was charged with conspiracy to commit mail and wire fraud (D. Colo., 1:21-cr-00006-RM) over employees in a data unit selling consumer data linked to clients running fraudulent mass-mailing schemes from about 2008 to 2017. A court-approved deferred prosecution agreement set $150 million, of which $127.5 million goes to victims. A search summary, not an opened page, reports a separate $42 million KBM Group agreement and later convictions of two former staff.
atlas_use: The strongest government record on Epsilon, showing marketing-data sales causing direct consumer harm. Open the KBM and conviction records before citing those parts.

title: Police Are Buying Access to Hacked Website Data
finding: SpyCloud sells law enforcement access to breached passwords, email addresses and IP addresses to generate investigative leads, according to webinar slides SpyCloud confirmed as authentic. One legal expert objects that this avoids legal process, the article notes it sweeps in people with no link to crime, and a child-protection investigator defends the practice.
atlas_use: Best evidence found of breach data becoming a commercial product. It concerns a breach-data vendor rather than a registered consumer data broker, so it should be labelled that way.
quote: unmask specific criminals and their personas

title: Inferring Tracker-Advertiser Relationships in the Online Advertising Ecosystem using Header Bidding
authors_or_outlet: Cook, Nithyanand, Shafiq; Proceedings on Privacy Enhancing Technologies 2020(1)
finding: Introduces Kashf, which infers data sharing from how advertiser bids change when specific trackers are present. It uncovers server-side relationships that cookie-sync detection misses and that external sources validate.
atlas_use: Supports the caveat that visible cookie syncing undercounts data sharing, so any atlas link map drawn from client-side observation is a lower bound.

title: CFPB Settles with Background Screening Company for $8.5M to Resolve Alleged FCRA Violations
finding: Summarizes a CFPB settlement of $6 million in consumer relief and a $2.5 million penalty. The bureau alleged incomplete or outdated public records, missing notices to consumers, and adverse items reported past the permitted period.
atlas_use: Enforcement entry for Sterling. The company name comes only from the linked CFPB PDF filenames, not the article body, so cite the consent order itself once opened.
quote: reported adverse information about consumers outside of the allowable reporting period

title: Cookie Synchronization: Everything You Always Wanted to Know But Were Afraid to Ask
authors_or_outlet: Papadopoulos, Kourtellis, Markatos; The World Wide Web Conference
finding: A year of web logs from 850 real mobile users shows 97% were exposed to cookie syncing, usually within their first week. Syncing multiplied the number of domains tracking each user by 6.75. The system built for the study also detects syncing when IDs are obfuscated.
atlas_use: Headline measurement and plain definition for cookie syncing, based on real users rather than crawlers. The sample is small and mobile-only.

title: Apollo Faces Criticism for Breach of 200 Million Contacts
finding: Citing TechCrunch, reports Apollo confirmed theft from a database of about 200 million contacts from 10 million companies, found weeks after July system upgrades. Apollo's customer email said most exposed data came from its publicly gathered prospect database.
atlas_use: Concrete harm for the B2B category: people who never dealt with the vendor were exposed. The critics quoted are security vendors.

title: Privacy Risks with Facebook's PII-Based Targeting: Auditing a Data Broker's Advertising Interface
authors_or_outlet: Venkatadri, Andreou, Liu, Mislove, Gummadi, Loiseau, Goga; IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
finding: Shows that custom-audience uploads can be exploited to infer full phone numbers from an email address and de-anonymise a website's visitors, at no cost and with no ad placed. Facebook acknowledged the issue and deployed a variant of the proposed fix.
atlas_use: Explains why customer-list onboarding, the route used by identity vendors, is itself a privacy-sensitive join. The specific attack has been fixed.

title: I never signed up for this! Privacy implications of email tracking
authors_or_outlet: Englehardt, Han, Narayanan; Proceedings on Privacy Enhancing Technologies 2018(1)
finding: Finds hundreds of third parties tracking email recipients, with about 30% of emails passing the recipient's address to at least one when viewed. Defences in 16 mail servers and clients were far from comprehensive.
atlas_use: Supports the point that email addresses leak to third parties on viewing. Any claim about hashing needs the full paper, because the abstract does not cover it.
quote: About 30% of emails leak the recipient's email address

title: Diffusion of User Tracking Data in the Online Advertising Ecosystem
authors_or_outlet: Bashir and Wilson; Proceedings on Privacy Enhancing Technologies 2018(4)
finding: Graph simulations estimate that 52 advertising and analytics companies could together observe at least 91% of an average user's browsing history under reasonable real-time bidding sharing assumptions. Major companies still saw 40 to 90% of impressions with blocking tools in use.
atlas_use: Quantifies concentration and the reach of bidstream data sharing. These are modelled bounds, not observed flows, and should be described that way.

title: CFPB Takes Action Under FCRA Against Employment Background Check Providers
finding: Two large employment screeners agreed to $10.5 million for consumers and a $2.5 million penalty. The CFPB cited no written procedures for common-name searches, not requiring middle names, weak dispute tracking, and stale records.
atlas_use: Shows a specific mechanism behind misattributed records. The body does not name the firms; General Information Services comes from the consent order link, and the affiliate is unconfirmed.
quote: the companies failed to follow reasonable procedures designed to ensure maximum accuracy

title: Criminal History Records: Additional Actions Could Enhance the Completeness of Records Used for Employment-Related Background Checks
authors_or_outlet: US Government Accountability Office (David C. Maurer), via Cornell eCommons
finding: The landing page describes the scope: FBI record checks by state, the completeness of state records, and how private companies run checks. It surveyed 47 states plus DC. The findings are not stated on the page.
atlas_use: Possible background on the record supply chain. Only the landing page was read, so read the PDF before citing any conclusion.

title: Selling Off Privacy at Auction
finding: Studies how ad companies exchange personal data through real-time bidding and cookie matching. It reports that a large share of browsing histories leaks to third parties and that individual history elements routinely sell for fractions of a cent.
atlas_use: Foundational evidence on the price and mechanics of bidstream leakage. The prices date from 2014, so it should be presented as historical.
quote: less than $0.0005

title: Matching Known Patients to Health Records in Washington State Data
finding: Washington sold a nameless patient-level hospitalization dataset for $50. Details from newspaper stories uniquely matched 35 of 81 sampled cases, about 43 percent, with a reporter confirming matches by contacting patients.
atlas_use: Concrete, replicable re-identification measurement on state-released data. Check its HIPAA status in the full paper before comparing it with HIPAA-standard de-identification, because the abstract does not state it.
quote: does not contain patient names or addresses

title: States Review Rules After Patients Identified Via Health Records
authors_or_outlet: Health Data Management, reprinting Bloomberg News
companies: IMS Health (now IQVIA) | OptumInsight | WebMD Health
finding: After re-identification work, Washington paused release of its database and several states began privacy audits or reviews. At least 26 states were said to sell hospital records with some identifying markers, and buyers named include IMS Health and OptumInsight. The page shows July 22 without a year; 2013 is inferred.
atlas_use: Shows state governments as an upstream source for health data brokers, outside HIPAA. The state counts are dated and need refreshing before publication.
quote: The goal here is not to stop data sharing.

title: FTC Fines Employee Background Screening Company $2.6 Million for Alleged FCRA Violations
authors_or_outlet: Hunton Andrews Kurth, Privacy and Cybersecurity Law Blog
finding: Law firm summary of a proposed $2.6 million FTC consent order over alleged failures on accuracy, including expunged records, consumer file access, dispute closure notices, and public record notification.
atlas_use: Enforcement entry for HireRight, which earlier sources covered only for ownership. Replace with the FTC record if available.

title: Building public trust in uses of Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act de-identified data
authors_or_outlet: Deven McGraw, Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association
finding: Data de-identified under HIPAA leaves the regulation and can be used for any purpose. The paper reports workshop discussion of concerns including no legal accountability for unauthorized re-identification and weak transparency, and says published evidence of re-identifying properly de-identified data is scarce.
atlas_use: Clear statement of the legal gap for a page explaining why de-identified health data can be sold, with the paper's own caveat.
quote: little published evidence of the re-identification

title: A Systematic Review of Re-Identification Attacks on Health Data
authors_or_outlet: El Emam, Jonker, Arbuckle, Malin, PLoS ONE 6(12)
finding: Across 14 attacks, about 34 percent of health records were re-identified on average, with a very wide confidence interval (0 to 0.744). Only one health attack targeted data de-identified to existing standards, and it succeeded at a rate of 0.00013. The authors say the evidence cannot settle how well de-identification works.
atlas_use: Necessary counterweight: it stops the atlas overstating how easily properly de-identified health data is reversed. Disclose that all authors declare consulting on de-identification for governments and commercial entities.
quote: evidence is insufficient to draw conclusions

title: Supreme Court Strikes Down Vermont Prescription Data Mining Law
finding: Reports that in Sorrell v. IMS Health, decided June 23, 2011, a 6-3 Court struck down under heightened First Amendment scrutiny Vermont's bar on drug companies buying or using prescriber-identifiable data for marketing. It suggests narrowly tailored privacy rules such as HIPAA could still be valid.
atlas_use: Key legal constraint on state limits to prescription data sale. The atlas should cite the slip opinion in No. 10-779 after retrieving it, and note this concerned prescriber data rather than patient identity.

title: How ComScore can track your mouse clicks
finding: Describes comScore panel software monitoring all internet behavior on the computer, including secure sessions, and possible matching of addresses to credit-agency data. It reports third parties installing it without proper consent. comScore said install requires affirmative consent, that it drops such partners and that it reports to clients in aggregate.
atlas_use: Historical context only: it is 18 years old and should not be used to describe current Comscore practice.
quote: there's nothing covert here

title: Credit-Based Insurance Scores: Impacts on Consumers of Automobile Insurance: A Report to Congress
finding: The FTC found the scores predict auto policy risk and differ across racial and ethnic groups, which likely affects average premiums. It also said only a relatively small share of predictive power comes from correlation with race and ethnicity, and it could not build an equally predictive model with smaller gaps. Only the summary page was read, not the report.
atlas_use: Baseline federal study on insurance scoring. Flag its age. Any statement that its method is contested needs a separately opened source.
quote: scores are effective predictors of risk under automobile policies

title: Trans Union's Sale of Personal Credit Information Violates Fair Credit Reporting Act, FTC Rules
finding: The FTC ordered Trans Union to stop selling target marketing lists to marketers lacking a permissible purpose, unanimously concluding the lists were FCRA consumer reports.
atlas_use: Foundational precedent for why bureau credit data cannot simply be sold for marketing. Historic; says nothing about current bureau marketing products.
quote: Trans Union's target marketing lists are . . . consumer reports under the FCRA

title: Availability of Sensitive Information About Consumers and Its Possible Use for Financial Fraud: Comments to the Federal Reserve Board
companies: TransUnion | LexisNexis | CDB Infotek | Information America | IRSC
finding: An early filing in Docket R-0953 describing header data as outside the FCRA, with no opt-out from sales to information vendors. It names Trans Union as the source for Lexis-Nexis's P-Trak service.
atlas_use: Historical anchor showing the header market and the opt-out gap date back to at least the 1990s. It predates GLBA, so use it for history only, not current law.
quote: The credit bureaus do not offer consumers the ability to
